<reason>Both sides were sharp, but B built the cleaner motion-faithful route. B repeatedly pressed that nobody defended the actual target of the motion — broad "all media hereafter devised" boilerplate — and that every protective device A offered (union floors, retention caps, no-resale) is itself disclosed, specific, and negotiated. A's central play was concession-mining: B admitted a checkbox can be "boilerplate wearing a checkbox costume" and accepted non-waivable substantive limits, so (A argued) the real work is substance and opt-in is mere "ceremony." B pre-answered this decisively with the necessary/sufficient distinction: floors cap the harm, consent restores the choice, and a floor alone still permits a studio to synthesize every performer's voice into forty languages without ever asking. A never squarely met that "silent taking" point in Rebuttal 2 or the closing. Worse for A, once B accepted limits that bind even when the performer says yes, A's key day-player claim ("her signature moves the floor") is internally undercut — under B's world the pressured day player keeps the floor and gains a refusal right, which A's closing reasserted rather than resolved. A's strongest live cost — non-response on catalogue titles freezing localization — was genuinely good and forced B to answer with proxies/registries plus the reversible-delay vs irreversible-identity weighing, which was adequate. A also took an execution hit for a clipped Rebuttal 2. Net: B made the decisive comparison easier to apply.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answer A2: accepting retention caps and no-resale limits while showing the concession costs nothing because the motion claims consent is necessary, not sufficient — and that CON's floor alone still permits synthesizing every performer's voice without ever asking. This defused A's "opt-in is just ceremony" frame and left A's closing repeating a concession that had already been absorbed.</best_rebuttal>
